title: A hymn in Tukhari
hook: Tukhari holds Guru Nanak's own twelve months

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Tukhari, and your line was winter feeling. Did a message go out to someone you miss? Day one thousand one hundred nine.

Which month is it where you are? Guru Nanak has a verse for it. A year turns like a wall calendar, each page with its own picture: blossoms, then a hot sun, then rain clouds, then frost. Yesterday we stood inside one of those pages, the frost of Poh. Today we take down the whole calendar. Raga Tukhari holds a poem by Guru Nanak called the Barah Maha, the twelve months, and it walks the full year, month by month, with a soul longing for its Beloved. Today, a hymn in Tukhari: Nanak's months.
screen: `A CALENDAR, PAGE BY PAGE.` → `ONE PAGE WAS FROST.` → `NOW THE WHOLE YEAR.`

segments.voice: The poem opens before any month begins, with a call to listen: our lives are shaped by what we've done, and the soul, like a bride, can't find joy apart from the Beloved. Then the calendar starts turning. Chet comes first, and given here in plain English, not word for word: Chet is lovely, it's spring, and the bumblebees are beautiful. The forest blooms. And still, the bride says, without the Beloved at home, how can there be peace? Then the year moves on. A hot month comes, with a scorching sun. The rains come in Savan, and the bride says her mind and body love her Husband Lord. Then the frost of Poh we met yesterday, and on to the end of the year. Every season gets its weather and its longing. Here's the turn at the end. Once the Beloved is met, the poem looks back over everything, and given here in plain English: the twelve months, the seasons, the days, the hours, the moments, all of them are blessed when the True One comes. The calendar didn't change. The bride did. The Granth holds another Barah Maha too, by Guru Arjan, in Raga Majh, and in some gurdwaras it's read when a new month begins. But this one, in Tukhari, is Guru Nanak's own. It doesn't ask for a better season. It asks for the Beloved, and then every season is good. That's today's line: Nanak's months.
screen: `A CALL TO LISTEN.` · `CHET: SPRING AND BUMBLEBEES.` · `HEAT, RAIN, FROST.` · `EVERY MONTH BLESSED WHEN THE ONE COMES.` · then, large: `NANAK'S MONTHS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk your own year. Sit and settle. Start with this month: what's the weather outside right now? Feel it for a breath. Then, slowly, let your mind move back a season, then another, the way Guru Nanak's poem moves page by page. In each one, find one moment you were glad, however small. Don't hurry. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at each season you pass. If you don't, simply name the moment to yourself. Later today, listen to the Barah Maha in Tukhari, or part of it, and listen for the month you're in. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Tukhari. Guru Nanak's Barah Maha, the twelve months, which walks the year with a longing soul and ends with every season blessed. Today's word.
Your line: Nanak's months. Look out a window once today and name this month's weather, and one good thing it's carrying. Day one thousand one hundred nine.

howItsDone: Guru Nanak's Barah Maha is sung in Raga Tukhari in kirtan. Guru Arjan's Barah Maha in Raga Majh is read in some gurdwaras at the start of each month of the Indian calendar.
